summary: RFC 5280 defines extended key purpose identifiers for X.509 certificates. This document defines additional identifiers for the Extended Key Usage extension in certificates used by Network Functions in the 5G System. Their uses include securing JSON objects in HTTP messages with JWTs and signing OAuth 2.0 access tokens.

eli5.summary: Certificates can say what a badge is allowed to do. This adds new badge labels so parts of a 5G network can show which jobs they may do.

subtitle: Three new certificate purpose labels so 5G network functions can prove a key is for signing tokens or encrypting JSON, and nothing else.

tldr.problem: Operators of 5G systems issue X.509 certificates to Network Functions for several jobs, but only client and server authentication had a standard purpose label. A certificate with no stated purpose could be misused for tasks its holder is not entitled to do.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three KeyPurposeIds for the Extended Key Usage extension: id-kp-jwt, id-kp-httpContentEncrypt and id-kp-oauthAccessTokenSigning. Each is paired with a required KeyUsage setting.
tldr.outcome: Certificates can now say whether their key signs a Client Credentials Assertion, encrypts JSON objects between SEPPs, or signs OAuth 2.0 access tokens. The IDs are standard, so they can be used outside 5G too.

today: RFC 9509 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2024, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. The text says the KeyPurposeIds are aimed at 5G but can be used in other deployments.

sections.title: The Problem in 5G Core Networks
sections.content:
Operators of 5G systems, as defined by 3GPP, run an internal PKI that issues X.509 certificates to Network Functions (NFs). The RFC lists four uses: client and server certificates for NFs in the 5G Core Service Based Architecture; signing the Client Credentials Assertion (CCA), which is a JSON Web Token secured with JWS; encrypting JSON objects in HTTP messages between Security Edge Protection Proxies (SEPPs) using JWE; and signing OAuth 2.0 access tokens that grant temporary access to resources offered by NF producers.

RFC 5280 already provides id-kp-serverAuth and id-kp-clientAuth, which can mark a certificate as belonging to a server (such as an NF service producer) or a client (such as an NF service consumer). There were no standard KeyPurposeIds for the other three uses.
sections.eli5: A 5G network has many small helpers, and each gets a badge. Only two kinds of badge label existed, so the badges for other jobs could not say what they were for.

sections.title: Why Unrestricted Certificates Are Risky
sections.content:
If a certificate does not restrict what its public key can be used for, it could be used for something other than intended, which raises the risk of cross-protocol attacks. The RFC says that using anyExtendedKeyUsage is generally considered poor practice, and especially so in 5G Systems and the 5GC Service Based Architecture.

It gives two examples. An NF service consumer could potentially impersonate NF service producers using its certificate. And an NF holding a client certificate and its private key must not be allowed to sign the CCA; the NF service producer should accept a CCA only if it was signed with a certificate explicitly issued for that purpose.

The RFC also argues against vendor-defined KeyPurposeIds. They are fine inside a vendor-controlled PKI, but using them outside that environment can cause interoperability problems, so standard ones are defined instead.
sections.eli5: If a badge does not say what it is for, someone could use their visitor badge to open the vault. Clear labels stop that.

sections.title: The Three New Key Purposes
sections.content:
The RFC defines three KeyPurposeIds: id-kp-jwt, id-kp-httpContentEncrypt and id-kp-oauthAccessTokenSigning. They are used, respectively, for signing the JWT Claims Set of the CCA using JWS, for encrypting JSON objects in HTTP messages between SEPPs using JWE, and for signing OAuth 2.0 access tokens using JWS.

Network Functions that verify a CCA signature, decrypt JSON objects between SEPPs, or verify an access token signature SHOULD require that the matching KeyPurposeId appears in the EKU extension. If the certificate requester knows its users are mandated to use these KeyPurposeIds, it MUST enforce their inclusion.

The requester must also make sure the KeyUsage extension is set to digitalSignature or nonRepudiation (also called contentCommitment) for signatures, and to keyEncipherment for secret key encryption.
sections.eli5: There are three new labels: one for signing identity tokens, one for locking up messages between gateways, and one for signing access passes. The checker should look for the right label before trusting a badge.

sections.title: Putting Them in a Certificate
sections.content:
The EKU extension from RFC 5280 is a SEQUENCE SIZE (1..MAX) OF KeyPurposeId, where each KeyPurposeId is an object identifier. The issuer may mark the extension critical or non-critical. The new identifiers sit under the existing id-kp arc as values 37, 38 and 39.

The RFC says that including these identifiers certifies the public key for three uses. First, validating the JWS signature in a JWT, where the distinction between JWS and JWE is made by KeyUsage: digitalSignature or nonRepudiation for JWS, keyEncipherment for JWE. Second, encrypting JSON objects in HTTP messages, for example encrypting the content-encryption key with the recipient's public key using RSAES-OAEP; KeyUsage is keyEncipherment. Third, signing OAuth 2.0 access tokens, with KeyUsage digitalSignature or nonRepudiation.
sections.eli5: The labels are written on the badge as special numbers from a big official list. Next to each label there is a second note saying whether the key is for signing or for locking.

sections.title: What a Certification Authority Must Do
sections.content:
A certification authority's procedures and practices MUST ensure the correct values for both the EKU extension and the KU extension are inserted in every certificate it issues.

Including the three new KeyPurposeIds does not rule out other KeyPurposeIds in the same certificate. RFC 5280 is quoted for the general rule: if the EKU extension is present, the certificate must only be used for one of the purposes indicated, and an application need not recognize every purpose listed as long as the intended one is present.
sections.eli5: The office that hands out badges must print the right job labels every time. A badge can carry more than one label if needed.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations of RFC 5280 apply. The RFC states that these key purposes do not introduce new security risks but reduce existing ones, by letting a relying party identify whether a certificate was issued to sign the JWT Claims Set, sign OAuth 2.0 access tokens, or encrypt the content-encryption key in JWE.

A relying party may also prohibit specific combinations of KeyPurposeIds, using the Excluded and Permitted KeyPurposeId procedure in Section 4 of RFC 9336. Examples of excluded cases are the presence of anyExtendedKeyUsage or a missing EKU extension. Examples of permitted ones are the presence of the three new identifiers.

On privacy, the EKU extension helps an observer determine what a certificate is for. In TLS 1.2 certificates are sent in the clear, while TLS 1.3 encrypts them. If the certificate comes from a public certification authority, an attacker could watch Certificate Transparency logs to learn its purpose.
sections.eli5: Clear labels make it harder to misuse a badge. The small catch is that anyone who can see the badge can also read its labels.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the three OIDs in the "SMI Security for PKIX Extended Key Purpose" registry (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3) as decimal values 37, 38 and 39. It also registered the ASN.1 module identifier id-mod-nf-eku as decimal 108 in the "SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier" registry (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.0).

Appendix A gives the ASN.1 module, which simply defines the id-kp arc and the three new values under it.
sections.eli5: The official number list now has three new entries, 37, 38 and 39, so everyone uses the same numbers for the same jobs.
